title: The Smoke Plume
subtitle: A warehouse fire sends smoke over the hub; a “toxic gas” post starts a stampede
coldOpen: 14:05. A paint warehouse behind the hub catches fire.
14:30. A post says the smoke is a nerve agent.
Commuters are running from the hub in every direction.

briefing.grievance: Commuters and nearby residents want to know whether the air is safe and why a chemical warehouse sat next to the busiest station in the city. Nobody has told them anything.
knownFacts: The warehouse stored paint and solvents; the fire service has it contained.
The pollution board’s monitor at the hub shows elevated particulates, no toxic agents.
Twelve people were treated for smoke inhalation; none are critical.
unverifiedClaims: A post with a video says the smoke is a nerve agent and people are collapsing.
A message says the city evacuated officials first.
briefing.responsibility: You run the emergency response and public information for the hub. Fear is moving faster than the smoke.
briefing.objective: Get accurate air readings out, keep the hub moving safely, and find out why the warehouse was there.

decisions.title: Running from the hub
decisions.situation: Thousands are leaving the hub at once. Three people have fallen on the stairs. The air monitor shows smoke, no toxins.

options.title: Broadcast the air readings every five minutes
options.preview: Loudspeakers, screens and the hub’s app repeat the monitor numbers.
options.authority: Duty of candour: say what is known and what is not
options.consequence: People hear a number instead of a rumour. The stairs clear.

options.title: Marshal the exits and slow the surge
options.preview: Staff and police open all exits and guide the flow.
options.authority: Duty to keep essential services running
options.consequence: The crush eases. Nobody else falls.

options.title: Seal the hub and stop all trains
options.preview: Gates lock; trains halt; thousands are held inside with the smoke.
options.authority: Article 19(2)–(3): restrictions must be reasonable and specific
options.consequence: People are locked in with the thing they fear.

delayed.message: The crackdown hardens people who had stayed out of it. More arrive, angrier.

options.title: Let the surge run its course
options.preview: No announcement; the video keeps playing.
options.consequence: Two more people fall on the stairs.

rightsMoments.question: A fire has caused panic. Can the city evacuate a kilometre around the hub “to be safe” when readings show no toxic agent?

options.text: No. Emergency powers still require a real, assessed risk and the least disruptive measure that meets it.
options.feedback: Correct. Proportionality applies in emergencies too; a cordon around the actual hazard met the risk.

options.text: Yes. In an emergency any precaution is justified.
options.feedback: Precaution has limits; mass evacuation without an assessed risk creates new dangers.
Timing does not fix a measure that the facts do not support.

rightsMoments.principle: Emergency measures that restrict movement and livelihood must be proportionate to an assessed risk (Article 19 restrictions must be reasonable). The least disruptive effective measure comes first.
rightsMoments.why: The monitor showed no toxic agent; a cordon around the warehouse protected people without emptying the city.

simple.question: A fire caused panic. Can the city evacuate a kilometre around the hub when readings show no poison?

options.a: No. Even in an emergency, use the smallest step that fits the real risk.
options.b: Yes. In an emergency anything is allowed.

feedback.a: Yes! Match the step to the real danger.
feedback.b: No. Big steps without real reasons cause new harm.
feedback.c: Timing does not fix a step the facts do not support.

simple.principle: Even in emergencies, use the smallest step that matches the real danger.
